entries.title: DOJ Drops Its Bid to Force California to Segregate Disputed Ballots
entries.summary: The department's motion said California will have already irreparably "commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones."
entries.content:
By Safiyah Riddle

LOS ANGELES (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice on Friday moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration status could be verified.

The request to dismiss the case comes days after Republicans' significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list. California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government's request.

The case was at the forefront of President Donald Trump's administration's effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Trump has said are rife with illegal voting without providing evidence.

The Department of Justice remains enmeshed in litigation with immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what is says are suspected noncitizens. Another controversial suit it filed in Alaska at Trump’s direction before the election to block the victory of the Democrat in that state’s Senate race was swiftly dismissed by a federal judge. The administration is appealing that ruling but has yet to file a full brief at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.

California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably "commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones."

“The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary,” the motion said.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, previously argued in court that the lawsuit would be irrelevant after election day, because there would be no way to sequester the ones allegedly belonging to noncitizens. The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state's 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized.

Essayli said at the time the lawsuit was filed that his goal was to “safeguard the integrity of the election so it doesn't have an effect on the upcoming election."

“We want to stop the illegal voting. We don't want to chase it later,” he said outside of court the week before the election.

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California referred all questions to the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., which did not respond to an emailed request for comment on Friday evening.

California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections. Elections clerks around California in the week before the election were sent subpoenas to testify before grand juries slated to convene in November. It's not clear who is being criminally charged in those cases, but the department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his blistering order that separating ballots at that late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections.

The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.

entries.title: The Duality of Trae Young
entries.summary: Playing against his former team for the first time, the Wizards guard showed both flaws and greatness.
entries.content:
ATLANTA — Two jarring sounds marked the end of Trae Young’s homecoming at State Farm Arena: the clang of leather-on-iron as Young’s final shot bounced off the rim, and the piercing blare of the final horn, sealing the Washington Wizards’ 139-132 loss. At that very moment, Young found himself standing a few strides from the Atlanta Hawks’ bench, so that’s where the first hugs were dispersed.

Hawks coach Quin Snyder. Assorted ex-teammates and staffers. Team owner Tony Ressler and his family. Security guards he got to know during his nearly eight years in a Hawks uniform. Directly above Young, in the rafters, hung the five uniform numbers retired by the franchise, and where someday, maybe, his old No. 11 might hang as well.

“I didn’t really get to say goodbye when I left in that trade,” Young said of the January deal that sent him from the Hawks to the Wizards, “and then I didn’t get to see or talk to anybody for a long time. So that was nice.”

The duality of Trae Young, as they know well in Atlanta, means you accept his flaws as the cost of all the greatness he brings, and both sides were on display Friday night. He scored 23 points and dished out 10 assists, both slightly above his season averages, as the Wizards, with superstar big man Anthony Davis sidelined with an ankle injury, fought valiantly behind Young and Kyshawn George (33 points and seven assists).

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

But Young also committed eight turnovers, several of them leading to easy buckets for the Hawks, and the last of which, an errant pass with 1:06 left in the game with the Wizards down four, proved particularly crucial.

If Friday night was a referendum on Young’s standing with the Atlanta fans 10 months after the trade, the results were inconclusive. He was the face of the Hawks franchise for the better part of eight seasons, arguably the team’s biggest superstar (and inarguably its leading scorer) since Dominique Wilkins. And yet the franchise in January had no problem sending him off to the Wizards for CJ McCollum and Corey Kispert in what was essentially a salary dump.

The return of the one-time face of the franchise in another team’s uniform is commonplace enough in this itinerant era of professional sports as to be almost cliche: the pregame hugs, the video tribute, the warm ovation, the waves/blown kisses/heart finger-gesture to the crowd. Young, in fact, had already been through all that, when he returned to State Farm Arena in February with the Wizards for a game in which he did not dress.

This time, everything was muted. No video tribute. No standing ovation. Just a perfunctory reciting of Young’s name during pregame introductions, followed by a tepid ovation tinged with a few boos.

“Any time there’s a breakup with a team, it’s never 100%,” Young said Friday morning after the Wizards’ shootaround. “But I’ve got a lot of love for Atlanta. My daughter was born here. I have a lot of family here, a lot of friends. I still get a lot of love here, and I think that will forever be the case.”

Trae Young AP - 26311098194551 (4141x2761, AR: 1.50)The body of work Young has authored across his career puts him among elite company. In NBA history, he ranks third all-time in assists per game, behind only Magic Johnson and John Stockton, and he is the only other player, along with Oscar Robertson, to have averaged at least 25 points and nine assists per game over an entire career. On the other hand, he is also the NBA’s all-time leader in turnovers per game, at 4.2.

That duality also informed Young’s relationship with Hawks fans. It was a complicated one, as might be expected between a fan base starved for a title and a singular star who could only manage to get the team three-quarters of the way there. In some circles, it is still held against him that the Hawks, on draft day 2018, traded away the rights to No. 3 overall pick Luka Doncic in order to move back two spots and take Young at No. 5 (and gain a future first-round pick), as if Young had anything to do with that.

He almost singlehandedly lifted the franchise to national prominence, taking them to Game 6 of the 2020-21 Eastern Conference Finals — the deepest playoff run in franchise history. But when the Hawks failed to advance past the first round in any subsequent season, he took the bulk of the blame, hearing the same knocks he’s been hearing his whole career: too small, too ball-dependent, too little defense.

Young played only five games for the Wizards last season following the trade, through some murky combination of Young’s various ailments and the Wizards’ own reluctance, near the end of a three-year tank job, to rush him back. Nonetheless, in July they signed him to a four-year $213 million contract that was widely panned around the league.

Though he was the clear face of the franchise in Atlanta, what the Wizards are asking of Young is more complex. He’s neither their biggest superstar (that would be Davis) nor the franchise cornerstone (that would be rookie AJ Dybantsa). But at their home opener, it was Young whom the organization handed the microphone at center court, asking him to say a few words to welcome the fans to the dawn of the Wizards’s new era.

Mostly, what the Wizards are asking of Young is to be himself, but just a little less — to subjugate his ego, to dial back the heliocentric role he played in Atlanta in order to share the ball with the most talented collection of teammates he has ever played with, some of whom need to ball in their hands.

Trae Young AP - 26311094588490 (3642x2429, AR: 1.50)
Young’s usage rate was over 30% in five of his seven full seasons in Atlanta, peaking at a whopping 34.9 percent in 2019-20, but this year it’s at a career-low 24.5. He’s also taking roughly five fewer shots per game than his career norm. That isn’t accidental: the Wizards are asking Young to play off the ball more than he is used to in order to maximize Dybansta’s preternatural on-ball skills and downhill motor.

“Yeah, it’s an adjustment. But it’s not a tough one,” Young said Friday morning. Being willing to change, he said, “is not something I’ve had to learn. It’s something I’ve always done. I know my usage rate is down. That’s not a problem.”

Because of his still-elite playmaking abilities, Young generates more open shots and scoring opportunities for the Wizards’ younger players than they would have without him. But because of his size (6-foot-2) and defense, they have to surround him with plus defenders. That’s the duality of Trae Young.

“I like what he’s giving us,” Wizards Coach Brian Keefe said of Young’s defense. “We obviously have some size behind him to protect him. And were doing things schematically to put him in position to be successful. But his mindset has actually been terrific. I like the effort he’s put out there. He’s got an ability to steal the ball. He’s been doing that for us, disrupting the game, because he knows he’s got people behind him to protect him.”

After Friday night’s loss, Young referenced his turnovers, saying, “I didn’t take care of the ball well enough today.” But he also dismissed all of his stats as secondary to his main task.

“I want to focus on the young guys and getting them the ball,” he said. “I know I’m going to have my time, and I’ll be aggressive. There are times I’ll have really good nights. But my main focus is not that. It’s how to help our young guys play well in winning situations…. We’re going to be in a lot of them this year.”

entries.title: Capitals Rally for a 4-3 Win Over Florida
entries.summary: Washington's Tom Wilson was ejected for a hit on Sandis Valmanis, but the Capitals rallied in the second.
entries.content:
By Noah Trister

WASHINGTON (AP) — Alex Tuch and Aliaksei Protas scored in the second period to lift the Washington Capitals to a 4-3 victory over the Florida Panthers on Saturday.

Brady Tkachuk scored two goals for the Panthers in the first, the latter coming on an extended power play after Washington's Tom Wilson was ejected for a hit on Sandis Valmanis, but the Capitals rallied in the second.

Jack St. Ivany scored his first career goal for the Capitals in the first, and Pierre-Luc Dubois added one in the third. Sam Bennett brought the Panthers within one with 46.6 seconds to play.

Valmanis did not return after Wilson's hit to his back knocked him headfirst into the area where the boards and glass meet. Wilson was given a major penalty for boarding, and Tkachuk put Florida ahead 2-1.

Tuch tied it with his 11th goal of the season, and then Washington took the lead with a nice team goal. Ryan Leonard battled behind the net and sent the puck to Dubois in the left circle. He made one more pass to Protas on the right doorstep, and he had an open net to shoot at.

Protas returned the favor in the final period with an assist to Dubois.

St. Ivany opened the scoring 2:21 into the game with a soft shot from the right boards that slipped past goalie Akira Schmid. Tkachuk answered less than a minute later after Washington's Dylan Strome turned the puck over in the defensive zone. It was Tkachuk's ninth goal of the season, and he'd add one more before the period was over.

Up next

Panthers: At Boston on Sunday.

Capitals: At Ottawa on Tuesday night.

entries.title: U.S. Fires on Commercial Vessel That Visited an Iranian Port
entries.summary: Iranian state media also reported the sound of explosions on an island in the Strait of Hormuz.
entries.content:
JERUSALEM (AP) — U.S. Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port.

U.S. forces have been enforcing a naval blockade on Iran for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial strategic waterway for shipping, including of oil. The last confirmed U.S. strike on a cargo vessel was nearly a month ago in the Gulf of Oman.

Saturday’s disclosure comes in the wake of at least two instances in which U.S. Central Command did not announce military strikes it has taken in the region and officials at the command declined to confirm strikes when asked about local reports of explosions.

Iran state media also reported on Saturday evening the sound of explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several explosions in the port of Jask. It wasn’t immediately clear what the cause of the explosions was and the U.S. military didn't immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment.

U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. military had carried out new limited strikes against Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system. Trump described the military action to reporters as “minor.” U.S. Central Command ultimately didn’t comment on the action even after the strikes were confirmed by Trump.

For weeks now, Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections. The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months.

Associated Press writer Konstantin Toropin contributed from Washington.
